The Nine Arch Bridge in Ella, Sri Lanka is a celebrated colonial-era railway viaduct also called the Bridge in the Sky. It was completed in 1921 and built entirely of stone, brick, and cement without steel reinforcement, a creative adaptation due to steel shortages during World War I. Wikipedia+1 The bridge spans about 91 m (300 ft) with nine elegant arches rising approximately 24 m (80 ft) above a lush jungle valley, set among tea plantations and misty hills. Lanka Pradeepa+1 It remains fully operational, carrying trains between Ella and Demodara stations, and is one of Sri Lanka’s most photographed attractions. Wikipedia Decorative nighttime lighting has been installed recently to let visitors appreciate the bridge after dark, enhancing tourism experiences. Train times passing the bridge - 6.30am, 9.30 am, 11.30 am, 3.30 pm, 4.30pm, 5.30pm

Visiting the Nine Arches Bridge was one of the highlights of my trip to Ella. Tucked between lush green hills and surrounded by tea plantations, this colonial era railway bridge feels like something out of a storybook. It's not just a photo opportunity  it’s a place where history, engineering, and nature come together beautifully. The walk to the bridge is half the experience. Depending on where you start (from Ella town or from the small road near the Art Café Umbrella), the trail takes about 20–30 minutes. The path winds through quiet jungle trails, small home gardens, and tea fields. It’s a peaceful walk and not very difficult  just wear proper shoes if it has rained, as it can get muddy. When you finally reach the bridge, the first view is breathtaking. The Nine Arches, built entirely out of brick and stone without any steel, stretch out across a deep gorge. Trains still run across it a few times a day and if you can time your visit to see one passing over, it’s a magical moment. We arrived just before a train was scheduled and sat with some locals and travelers on the hillside. Everyone fell quiet when the train appeared — slowly curving across the bridge with its horn echoing through the valley. It felt timeless, almost like stepping into a slower, simpler world. Tips: Best time to visit: Early morning or just before sunset fewer crowds and better light for photos. Train times: Ask a local or your guesthouse; trains aren’t always on schedule. For photos: Walk up the little hill opposite the bridge for a great angle with the forest in the background. There are cafés nearby if you want to enjoy a tea or juice with a view. Be respectful  it's still an active railway and also a quiet area for locals. Nine Arches Bridge isn’t a long visit  maybe an hour or two  but it leaves a lasting impression. It’s a peaceful, scenic break from busier tourist sites, and it connects you to the charm of Sri Lanka’s hill country in the most beautiful way.

The Nine Arches Bridge, nestled in the scenic town of Ella in Sri Lanka, is a remarkable feat of engineering and a symbol of the island’s natural beauty and colonial past. Completed in 1921 during British rule, this iconic railway bridge spans 91 meters in height and stretches over 300 meters in length, arching gracefully across a lush, verdant valley. Its structure, characterized by nine large arches, is an awe-inspiring example of early 20th-century engineering, built using solid bricks and concrete without the use of steel. The bridge is strategically placed within a landscape of dense forests, rolling hills, and tea plantations, which offers visitors breathtaking panoramic views that have made it one of Sri Lanka's most photographed landmarks. As a key part of the railway line that connects Colombo to Badulla, the Nine Arches Bridge serves not only as a transportation route but also as a historical relic. The surrounding area, rich in biodiversity and serene beauty, has made it a prime destination for nature lovers, adventurers, and photographers. The bridge is often seen as a peaceful contrast to the hustle and bustle of urban life, offering a glimpse into Sri Lanka's colonial heritage. Tourists flock to this bridge to marvel at its intricate design and its ability to blend harmoniously with the surrounding natural environment. Whether visited during the misty mornings or the golden hours of sunset, the Nine Arches Bridge never fails to leave a lasting impression on those who encounter it. It remains an enduring symbol of Sri Lanka’s cultural and natural heritage, standing as a testament to the resilience of both the human spirit and the land it inhabits.

I hired a private driver and requested to visit here as one of my stops. There is a car parking lot near the bridge (you have to walk a short distance from it to get to the bridge) but several kilometers away from the parking lot, the driver stopped and claimed that he couldn't go farther on the road and I would need to take a tuk tuk the rest of the way or walk 30 minutes. He said the tuk tuk would cost around 1,000 LKR but the only tuk tuk at the spot refused anything less than 1,500 LKR. Since I was already overpaying for the private driver I balked and it was at that point the driver told me he'd see how far he could go down the road. Spoiler alert: he got all the way to the parking lot. More than any other place I visited in Sri Lanka, the tuk tuk drivers in Ella seem to have a real racket going and you can't even trust that your private driver or tour guide won't try to feed you to these guys. But if you do try to get to Nine Arches by car, know that it is possible to get to a parking lot that is a short walk from the bridge and don't let a driver try to tell you otherwise.

How many stone arch bridges (namely stone, without the use of reinforced concrete and other iron) do you know? Until I wrote this post, I didn’t really bother with this issue. It turns out that there are more than enough of them - STONE bridges in the world. True, there are not so many bridges made of stone, whose arched spans are at least 50 meters. Surely you have heard of the Juxigou Bridge in China, the Maidenhead Viaduct in England, the Solkan Bridge in Slovenia, the Heather Bridge in Iran, the Wiesen Viaduct in Switzerland, the Pont de Vieille Briude in France, etc. In total, I managed to count about six dozen wide-span bridges around the world. In reality, there are many times more stone bridges with narrow spans. But they are no less interesting, take the word of an old travel lover!!! But!!! How many of these STONE bridges are railway bridges? Even clever Wikipedia couldn’t answer this for me. During my trip to Sri Lanka, I was able to get acquainted with the local must see, which represents one of the best examples of colonial-era railway construction in Ceylon. Moreover, as they say, “three in one”: this is a BRIDGE, it is STONE and it is RAILWAY!!! I'm talking about the Nine Arches Bridge - the Bridge of Nine Arches. It is built across a swampy lowland near the village of Gotuwala between two railway stations - Ella and Demodara. This bridge is one of the favorite places for party-juice of insta-people: 9 out of 10 travel lovers will definitely not fail to visit this object to photograph the architectural ingenuity of the creators of the Bridge and the abundant tropical greenery on the nearby hillsides, and then post their smiling photo in the virtual world. For lovers of historical and engineering precision, the Nine Arches Bridge is a pain in the ass: only its dimensions are known from accurate information (length - 91.44 meters, width - 7.62 meters, height - 24.38 meters). AND THAT'S ALL!!! As for the time of its construction: according to one piece of information, work on the construction of the bridge began in 1912, according to another - a year later. If you believe some sources, the completion date of the mega-construction is 1921, others claim that it is 1923. At least a report entitled "Construction of a Concrete Railway Viaduct in Ceylon" was published by the Ceylon Engineering Association in 1923. Most guidebooks, as a rule, attribute the construction of the bridge to the local Ceylonese builder P.K. Appukhami in “co-authorship” with some British engineers. In fact, there is a funny legend circulating regarding Comrade Appuhami and his role in the construction of the bridge. Evil tongues claim that he is not a builder. Allegedly in 1912, the popular drummer and performer of “devil dances” (yakṣa næṭuma) in Ceylon P.K. Appuhami was returning with another panty in the lift of that same Devil-Yaksha (Yakṣayā). At the station in Ohiya, he came across a certain son of Foggy Albion, who almost “did not move his horses” from fright, seeing the Yaksha appearance of our Phil Collins, Dave Grohl and Cozy Powell of the Sri Lankan “spill” in “one bottle”. Thank God, the Briton did not “grunt” and through him Appuhami ended things with the bridge builders and, as some not very trustworthy sources say, received the unofficial status of the chief engineer of the project. Whether this is true or not - only the drummer himself knows... The chief designer and manager of the “Railway Line to Ceylon” project was D.J. Vimalasurendra, supposedly another eminent Ceylonese engineer and inventor. The designer of the viaduct is said to be Harold Cuthbert Marwood of the Railway Construction Department of the Ceylon State Railway. And another epic Aboriginal tale associated with the personality of P.K. Appuhami: British engineers, led by the mentioned Mr. Marwood, have completely broken their heads, excuse the tautology - how to install 9 columns in the swampy quagmire of a valley? And then again - and like a jack-in-the-box, that same Appukhami!!! Ceylon drummer proposed an ingenious move, like “cowards worth a ruble or forty,”: throwing huge boulders into the depression until they fill it. And on this “piled foundation” the columns were then installed!!! The huge bridge is located at an altitude of 945 meters above sea level, which is why its second name is “Bridge in the Sky”. By the way, the uniqueness of this railway bridge beauty lies in the fact that it is entirely built from rocks, bricks and cement - without the use of steel or iron!!! And again, another story: when construction work began, the First World War broke out almost immediately. And, quite expectedly, the front needed iron... It seems that everything is clear: no material - no bridge!!! But the skillful Ceylonese peasants took and built the Bridge from bricks, cobblestones and cement. Without iron, therefore... How long can you do it skillfully? And now - from the realm of mysteries and mysticism... When I saw the Nine Arches Bridge, I was struck by the feeling of that same déjà vu: I have already seen this building!!! Well, or something very, very similar!!! Of course: Istanbul's Bozdogan, Tarragona's "Devil's Bridge", Rome's Parco degli Acquedotti... And what do we get? Dear Sri Lankan bridge builders, I suppose, who had no idea about antiquity, simply erected a unique arched bridge in the style of ancient Roman viaducts without any iron load-bearing elements, using only stone, brick and cement??? A masterpiece of bridge construction based on technology a couple of millennia old??? Do you believe this yourself, my dear reader??? Go ahead. Ella (Sinhala: ඇල්ල, lit. 'fall'; Tamil: எல்ல) is a small town in the Badulla District of Uva Province, Sri Lanka governed by an Urban Council. It is approximately 200 kilometres (120 mi) east of Colombo and is situated at an elevation of 1,041 metres (3,415 ft) above sea level.[2] The area has a rich bio-diversity, dense with numerous varieties of flora and fauna. The Ella Gap allows views across the southern plains of Sri Lanka.[3]

Eighteen of us, travelling together with Flamingo Tours, visited the Nine Arch bridge on 10th September 2023.  After visiting Demodera Railway Station, we hired tuk-tuks up to the bridge site - about five kilometres as the approach is not motorable by car. This railway bridge, constructed in 1921, entirely of stone bricks and cement, lies between Ella and Demodera railway stations.  It joins two hills along the rail line and is 80 - 100 feet high and 300 feet long. The bridge itself, bathed in morning sunlight, was a breathtaking sight at both ends.  We walked along the rail line, atop the bridge to the far side and back.  On either side of the bridge are little kiosks that sell king coconuts and other fruits. We were amongst a large crowd of tourists awaiting the arrival of the train.  Seeing the approaching train on this concave shaped nine arch bridge was certainly a memorable and a wonderful sight.  The train came slowly, allowing the visitors to capture photos of it on the concave bridge, before disappearing into the tunnel beyond.

Make sure you know how to get there because there are multiple ways to get to the bridge and you'll be lost if you don't choose the right path. I wish Lonely Planet has covered this more thoroughly.  There are not enough signs to show you how to reach this point and definitely not enough coverage about how steep and slippery the slope could be on the way to the bridge.  Hope whoever reading this will find the following tips helpful: 1) If you take the entrance near 98 Acres, the entrance has a mini colorful Hindu shrine and a coconut stand. Follow the signs and walk uphill until you reach a fork with no sign in the middle of the hill, take the left fork that will bring you through a muddy path and keeps walking for another five min or so before you can see the bridge below you on the far left.  I was told there are other ways to get there but this path brings you to the classic instagram shot of the bridge when the train hits. 2) If you choose to take this path, then beware of a very slippery muddy slope. It was drizzling when we were in the middle of walking toward the nine arch bridge. Both my partner and I were in sneakers and we were slipping and almost fell on a few occasions when we tried to climb down the slope.  Many people also found it challenging towards the end. I am a 5 feet 2 Asian who rarely exercised. I managed to get down in one piece using an umbrella as a hiking stick and towards the end I had to rely on my hand on the ground to keep myself from slipping a few times.  I also had help from my partner and a few kind tourists.  I would feel a lot safer with trekking shoes and a hiking stick, and I would not recommend visiting this place if it is raining. 3) Try to ask your hotel for the train schedule. The experience was so much more fun with the train passing by with passengers waving and cheering. A few brave tourists sat on the bridge when the train passed by.  It took me about 50 minutes to walk from 98 Acres resort to the bridge.  On the day I went, which was a Sunday, I was told trains would pass through the bridge around 9:20am, 1:45pm and 3:15pm.

You can ask the locals and they will be able to help you with the exact time of train crossing through the bridge. Trains are almost always on time. My wife, our grandson Ryan and I, left our car at Ella Railway Station on 23rd July 2019 and hired a tuk-tuk to see the Nine Arch Bridge.  The road to the bridge is in bad state of disrepair and narrow with sharp curves.  Although we hired a tuk-tuk, one can walk from the Ella station, along the railway line, to the Nine Arch Bridge, a distance of about 3 kilometers. There are only a few trains plying this route.  The tuk-tuk driver hurried along to be in time to show us the train crossing over the bridge.  The bridge, as the name suggests, is built over nine arches atop tall walls, and runs over the 100 ft deep ravine.  It is called the "sky bridge" emphasising the depth of the ravine.  On that beautiful sunny morning, it was a wonderful sight to observe the train moving over this unique bridge. The train moved slowly over the bridge allowing me to capture a few attractive photographs. The bridge had been commissioned in 1921, built during the British Rule.  The world war I broke out while it was being built.  The consignment of steel earmarked for the bridge was diverted to the army for projects associated with the war.  If steel were available, the bridge could have been built with only two or three spans across the ravine.  Since there was no steel available, the engineers incorporated eight shorter spans supporting the bridge over these nine convex arches.  Blocks of stone joined together with cement were the sole construction materials used in its construction. On its journey from Ella to Demodera the railway line passes through a 60 metre long tunnel about 75 metres after the arch bridge.  Don’t miss out on taking a photo with you at the entrance to the tunnel!  There were many excited tourists watching the train moving along!! The tuk-tuk driver Rathnayake (QP8422) dropped us at Demodera Railway Station for our train ride back to Ella after seeing the famed Demodera Loop.

The lady vendor was doing very brisk business here as there were lots of sightseers waiting for the train. It was very rewarding to then watch the train traverse the bridge, especially as we didn't time it so, it was purely by chance for us. Amazed by just how long it then was! Back then and quite a steep uphill climb on the return. Our guide was very proud of the Nine Arches Bridge - it's a lovely spot and stunning piece of architecture but we didn't have the heart to tell him about Ribblehead which has 24 arches.

We only viewed the bridge from the train as we passed over it however, from a restricted viewpoint it looked great. Fortunately the train was going quite slowly at the time but our photos simply don’t do it justice. We intended to walk up from Ella to see it the next morning but ran out of time as we left early.

This a beautiful beautiful bridge, it's a must in Ella and we couldn't recommend it more. Due to the amount of tourists we went early so we could get less crowded pictures. We had a scooter still through the morning so turned left from Ella main road and followed the signs through little roads until we got to a house garden which let us park our scooter there. From there it was a 2min to the bridge, we were there at 6.30am as there was a train passing by between 6.30am and 7am and is definitely something worth watching. Train passed at 7am and although there was some ppl there we got some great shots ! Totally recommend and advise to go early ! Also if you don't have a scooter you can follow the tracks by foot. Many locals are willing to point you in the right direction any time you need!

A great attraction to visit if you are in the Ell area.  The bridge itself is a spectacular viaduct across a deep ravine. When there are no trains you can walk over the bridge quite safely and enjoy the views.  Worthwhile finding out when the next train is due as this will create much excitement and more photo opportunities.

It’s well worth a visit and it’s absolutely beautiful. However be careful if you see a drone because there are bees nests underneath the bridge and I think the drone aggravates them. We got stung so bad and everyone was running around screaming in absolute panics! The locals and police told everyone to run in the tunnel for cover which did stop the bees eventually and they lit a fire to scare them away but it was a mad 5 minutes. This doesn’t take away how beautiful this place was and it’s truly well worth a visit just be mindful, wear insect repellent and maybe cover up as much as you can.

Yes it’s just a bridge, and yes it’s just a train going across, and yes there’s going to be other people there.... but it’s a must do in Ella, and way better than it sounds! In short, the bridge is actually really beautiful at sunset, sunrise, and during the day (the latter having the most people) #1 - Make sure you know when the trains are coming. Check Gov website or Seat61 #2 - Make sure you take the time to see both viewpoints (both are on the west side of the bridge, one north, one south) #3 - There are plenty of locals selling coconuts, and a handful of little cafes selling drinks too so you don’t necessarily need to take your own. #4 - The best way to get there is via Passara Road (best viewpoint but it’s not flat) - scenic and #5 - The worst way to get there is via the train tracks at Ella Station (bit boring but you won’t get lost). Summary - do it, but take note of the above! Ignore any reviews from people who go to see a bridge but expect a rollercoaster.

Based on the information received by our hotel, we thought there were only a few (two) trains going by every day and taught we had missed our chance of seeing it. However, our tuck-tuk driver informed us that there would be another train coming from the opposite direction within 30-45 minutes so we waited a bit and saw the train going on the 9 arch bridge while sipping a fresh coconut juice from a coconut that this merchant was opening right on the spot. Nice! We came from 98 Acres hotel ( from the road took a tuk-tuk, then needed to walk a bit downhill and thereafter on the railroad tracks). Some other viewers came from the other side of the arch bridge but were making their way to our side...so I think the view is better when coming from the road passing 98 Acres hotel.

One of the first things we wanted to do in our stay in Ella. A short tuctuc ride (my girlfriend wasn't feeling well so we didn't go for the full walk from the town itself) and a short walk from there to the bridge itself. The walk is relatively easy but make sure you bring shoes that can handle slippery, muddy paths with the occasional steep descends. The view is worth it just don't think you will have a quiet time taking it all in as it's likely to be swarmed by tourists from start to finish. We've had people with drones (which aren't allowed due to aggressive bees under the bridge), whole groups making all kinds poses on the tracks to couples taking photosessions in the thea fields below. I think it's a must see but be prepared to share your trip with half the world :-p

I was looking forward to seeing this bridge and it didn't disappoint! After a walk through the jungle to get here we arrived to get some good pictures just before a train came along, we then walked along the trainline back to Ella.

Beautiful bridge located over the tea plantations. We really enjoyed visiting it. However we were unlucky and not train came at that time. There's a train at 15:30 and I am sure that the experience is a lot better if you get to see the bridge with a train on it.

As it is not well described in many travel guides (looking particularly at you, Lonely Planet), many seem to think the best way to get to the Nine Arch Bridge is to either hire a TukTuk or to walk on the train tracks from Ella Station (would you ever take a stroll on in use train tracks at home?!). There’s however a better third option: A 10 minuets easy walk via a forest path, starting off the main road leading to Little Adams Peak (see map). The path is good and leads through some nice piece of forest, where you even might spot some monkeys and you will also get a view of the bridge from the top. The bridge itself is picturesque, but swamped with masses of tourists and ultimately nothing too special. But given that there’s overall not too much else to see in Ella, the bridge is probably worth a visit. And if only to observe the acrobatics of tourists on the bridge balustrade high above the ground in hunt for the perfect selfie or vain mothers more focused on their iPhones than on their toddlers, who in the meanwhile go off to irritate the stray dogs...

The best way to experience the 9 arch is whilst a train travels across anyone who did the long train trip Kandy to Ella (standing) will know it’s a long train ride but worth the views and to experience it from outside the train you must get to the bridge for around 3:30 to see the train travel across like this

One of the most beautiful places to visit in Ella! It provides amazing views and plenty of opportunities to take photos of yourself and friends/ family on the railway tracks with the vast vegetation around it. Lovely bridge, can be viewed from a few places- actually on the tracks, through the jumble to trek below the bridge and another road/track to view above the bridge. We walked from the edge of Ella having just climbed Little Adam's peak - stopped for lunch at Ella Flower Garden Resort. The nine arch bridge is a must visit in Ella. From the viewpoint, the bridge is about ~5-10 mins downhill walk. The path leading to the bridge is slightly rocky so would recommend some shoes as opposed to jandals. There is a very nice locally run juice bar at the viewpoint (very cheap, freshly squeezed juices and smoothies with ice cream). The juice bar has a train schedule detailing when the train will arrive on the bridge for those waiting for the Insta shot. Highly recommend!

We found tip to reach bridge by path leading through jungle and we were really happy with decision to follow it in the end. It is 10 min walk downhill through wild forest, so you have chance to see some tropical plants and also houses build in jungle hills. There are basically no tourists and it is actually the shortest way as well. Take turn leading into forest after parking lot next to Umbrella art Cafe!

For some reason this railway bridge is quite an attraction. Not unlike any other arched bridge across a valley we walked there to find out why. It carries the trains from Kandy through Ella and beyond but there was nothing about it of any significance. Perhaps the one thing different to most railways was that you could walk through the railway tunnel back to Ella by way of the railway lines. Worth a visit just to say you have done this.

A little bit of a trek down a rough track brings you to a cafe with outdoor seating. Some of the benching( odd bits of wood) look a bit suspect, but they’re OK ( don’t think H&S UK style: barriers, warning notices). Just a short walk from the bottom of Adam's Peak to Nine Arch Bridge. Loads of people gather here to watch the trains, even though they only pass by every few hours. Was really looking forward to visiting this bridge. We tried to follow signs from Little Adam’s Peak but the signs just seemed to stop at one point. It seems you walk past the Newburgh green tea factory and down the hill that way. The path from the view point down to the track looked more like a dried up stream bed which was incredibly dry and slippy. When walking to the bridge a local young man told us we were going the wrong way and we felt pretty confused. We continued on the way we were going and then heard him and his friend following us down the hill which was intimidating. The young man then said we had come down the wrong bit and he would show us how to get down to the viewing point and we had to be quick as a train was coming in five minutes. He chatted to us and seemed pleasant and took us to a viewing point. We wanted to get to the tracks so he said he would point us in the right direction. We figured he would expect some money but then he started up a learnt spiel about the fruit growing and the tea plant as he walked us up. At the top he demanded 2500 rps!! We were pretty upset afterward as this experience tarnished our visit to the bridge and made me distrustful of other people in Sri Lanka, who to that point had all been lovely. The Nine Arch Bridge is one of the best examples of colonial-era railway construction in the country. The designer of the viaduct was Harold Cuthbert Marwood of Railway Construction Department of Ceylon Government Railway. Popular rumors suggest that when construction work commenced on the bridge, the Great War began between the empires of Europe and the steel assigned for this site was reallocated to Britain's War related projects at the battlefront. As a result, the work came to a standstill, leading the locals build the bridge with stone bricks and cement, but without steel.

It goes against the grain to walk along railway tracks, especially for a few miles but it is the norm in Ella despite signs telling you not to. There are two trails that you could take. One (as I heard) a longer and tedious route and the one we took, the shorter route, directly leading to a nice viewpoint (downwards from the confusing junction). The shorter one is recommended by many villagers - probably to avoid leeches (not a fan of them clinging on to me). The trail is clear and there is a not too difficult downward slope. However, if it does rain, it could get slippery. Not too cold or windy but the area is often misty and is known for unpredictable rains so it would be best to take a jacket to be on the safe side. Once you reach the viewpoint, there's a small cafe - #asangacafe where tea and snacks are served by the friendliest villagers you'll meet. Stunning bridge with breathtaking views. Try and time your visit when a train is passing for an incredible experience and photos! Warning - I’d recommend taking a tuk tuk up to the bridge as cars can’t use the paths leading to it and it’s a bit of a walk!

This is a beautiful bridge set in the stunning jungle and tea fields around Ella. It is very scenic but unfortunately the place has become very touristic and is very crowded with people just trying to get the perfect photo to put on their social media accounts! It’s a shame, because when people are too focussed on the photo, they forget to enjoy the experience and can be very inconsiderate and rude to others around them. This is the type of crowd we unfortunately found at the bridge. To be honest, I would recommend taking advantage of Ella’s amazing scenery with some hiking but don’t make any effort to come to this bridge - just go and enjoy somewhere quieter away from the crowds!

This bridge is apparently an engineering marvel. Tourists walk the tracks from Ella to see the bridge and try to time it when a train is going through. We caught the train from Ella to Dambulla. It was 20 rupees for 2 tickets. We rode the train across the bridge. You cannot see the bridge but just depends what interests you. We got off the train in Demodora. There are always tuk tuks to take you back to Ella.

The photos you see on Instagram are ridiculously edited, but it’s still quite fun to visit it when a train passes over (they are very infrequent so check the timings first). Not much else to do nearby except a couple cafes (which we didn’t try). Suggest dropping by if you’ve hired a tuk tuk for the day or were doing a walk nearby. Go for one of the earlier trains as it will be less crowded.

This colonial architecture beauty is definitely a must visit place. Amidst rich jungle and little tea plants, this looks absolutely stunning. If you want to experience the train passing by it , then try to be here around 3-4 pm and then 6:30 pm. Generally, this time train passes by. Also, try to hike a little bit here and there to have picture perfect angle/view of this bridge.

The hike from Ella, through to Little Adam’s Peak and onto the Nine Arch Bridge is a great way to spend a morning! Start early to not only beat the heat but the crowds as well! You can wait for the train if you wish, but it’s an unreliable timetable so just enjoy the views and the scenery here instead!

We saved this for our last day. Easy walk along the tracks for about 25 minutes. We found a spot on the mountain to watch everyone on the tracks. It's worth the walk to see the train and the people. Check the timetable and get your spot!

We really enjoyed the walk on the tracks to the bridge (even though it is officialy forbidden, but nobody cares and everybody does it), A very nice walk für about 45 minutes. The bridge is fun and the setting quite spectacular. There is a nice walk past mini Adams Peak and the 98 Acres luxury resort set amid tea plantations to get to the cafe above the bridge. But for those who choose to actually get onto the bridge, beware as the way did  us steep and slippery AND while no one warns you about them, the place is wet and warm enough for there to be leeches lurking in the undergrowth. But it is an easy walk from the centre of Ella and well worth the trek.

It's a little bit of a pain to get to - first, from where a tuk tuk will drop you off (no signposting)... and then once you're at the view-point from above, there's a steep scramble down the hill to the bridge itself. However, it's very very picturesque, and a must-visit when in Ella - really beautiful. Would recommend taking in the views from above, but also going down to the bridge-level itself, walking across the bridge and along the tracks. Additionally, check the train timetable - good to visit when there are some trains scheduled, and you may be able to get a photo from the bridge-level, then under 30min later, a photo from above. As with most things in Sri Lanka, would recommend avoiding visiting during the heat of the day!

After a 30 minute walk or so from the Ella station we arrived at the bridge, it was already packed with people waiting for the perfect shot of the tracks with a train. As we arrived the train came through a few minutes later. It wasn't that special to be honest but nice to see.

The bridge is nice to see, but a not that easy to go there. You have to climb through tea fields down the hill. We weren't really intending on climbing down to the tracks, having read other reviews, but when it came to it, the climb down wasn't that bad. Ok, if it had been pouring down at the point we were doing it, we might have changed our minds, but as it was even our six year old managed perfectly well. We got a bit lost on the road after the cafe  and walked past the tiny path to the left but then retraced our steps and found it (although we weren't 100% it was exactly the right path!). About half way down we paused and waited for the train to come through to take some photos, then climbed down the rest of the way. It wasn't too busy as it was quite cloudy and there had been rain earlier. We walked through the tunnel, which the kids loved, and then headed off on a path to the right down to a small road. It's a bit disorientating as we weren't sure which way to go but worked out that right took you back to the opening of the tunnel (where the tuktuks were dropping off) and left took you back down to Ella. You can also walk back to Ella along the tracks, however we set off down the road and jumped into a tuktuk about half way back to Ella for the rest of the way.

The Nine Arches Bridge is a bridge in Sri Lanka (Demodara, between Ella and Demodara railway stations). It is one of the best examples of colonial-era railway construction in the country.The surrounding area has seen a steady increase of tourism due to the bridge's architectural ingenuity and the profuse greenery in the nearby hillsides. Ideal place for film shooting or wedding shooting. Wonderful place with lot of beautiful scenes.

The bridge is nestled in the hills and therefore was a bit hard to find - the signposts weren’t so clear to us, so it is worth looking up the route before you set off. We set off from Ella and walked up Little Adam's Peak then on to the Nine Arch in time for the train. Full of people on the track and watching from the viewpoints. You can hear the train coming and it's fun watching the guards continually whistle at people to clear the tracks.The train comes and goes for your photo opportunity. Yes you can take photos of the bridge and standing on the track with a whole host of tourists in the background and foreground. We did the walk back to Ella along the track. Not a very interesting walk. The novelty of walking on a train track goes pretty quickly. In the afternoon we caught the train from Ella to Demodara to experience going over the bridge. It was a holiday that day so the train was packed but the 25 minute journey in 2nd class cost 10Rp each. It was great fun riding the train with the locals and hearing the screams as we went through each of the tunnels. Get off at Demodara, cross the car park and watch the train you just got off go underneath you through the tunnel. Catch a tuk back to Ella for 600Rp. We saw the bridge from every angle - at a distance, walking on it and crossing it on the train. It is something you feel you have to do as it is so widely talked and written about but it certainly wasn't the highlight of my time in Sri Lanka. Demodara Nine arch bridge is a major tourist attraction at Ella. It is situated between Ella and Demodara stations more closer to Ella station. (3km along the railway track). There are few ways to reach the bridge. You can walk along the rail track from Ella station. There are two foot pathways from Ella town as well as Ella-Passara roads. And another mortable road (3W) from Ella town. Most fascinating thing is to capture a train over the bridge. Time table of trains which reach Ella station from Colombo side: 6.06am, 1.30am, 3.15pm, 5.30pm, 6.30pm and Time table of trains which reach Ella from Badulla side:6.39am, 9.23am, 12.04pm. There is a stunning bridge in Ella, Sri Lanka that is similar to Harry Potters railway viaduct (Glenfinnan Viaduct). It is known as Nine Arch bridge or Sri Lankan Harry Potter's Bridge. Nine Arch Bridge is one of a British railway constructions when Sri Lanka was a colony under the British Empire.The suggestion was given by a Sri Lankan worker, Appuhamy lived nearby. You can see breathtaking views, tea plantations, tunnels & also beautiful birds here. We walked along the railway tracks from Ella station for about 2kms leisurely. The bridge is just so beautiful.  We were there in the evening and it was a very pleasant walk on the tracks. We stayed for an hour waiting for the evening train to arrive. The views were spectacular, beautiful scenery and photo opportunities are also found. The splendid nine arch bridge is the main sight. It is simply incredible to see such a magnificent piece of architecture in the middle of no-where, surrounded by jungle. You can also climb up to higher ground to enjoy an aerial view of the bridge and track. We saw the train passed around 5.45 pm and that was a visual treat. The track back up was steep.  If you're lucky enough you can meet a running train just next to you. It is a very chilled place.     It is an old train model, very charming. Brings you back to the colonial era.It  is incredible to be able to get so up close, you can feel the draft as the train passes. Better pictures, however, can be taken from a higher perspective, from the hill.  Be careful when you climb down, a bit slippery, and can be challenging. After sighting the train, you can go back and have a nice meal at Ella, where we also had a wonderful experience. If you can get to know the train times, it is great as you get added enjoyment seeing it travelling on the 9 arched bridge if you happen to go in the morning or in the afternoon. However, if you don't want to walk, you can reach by car as far as the Hindu shrine (you can also park there and give some offering for the maintenance of the temple).  Then hire a tuk-tuk. It will take you there and back for only Rs 500. well worth the money. The ride was in itself an adventure. Be prepared for a rough ride with a tuk-tuk. From the shrine, with the tuk-tuk, it takes about 10 minutes to reach the hill leading down to the bridge.  Climb down the hill, following the pathway, until you reach the bridge and wait along with the others. The train also passes at different times, more or less about in every 3 hours. Around 9, 12, 15, and 18 (but better check the exact time from the station or from the “Trains – Sri Lanka App”). Children from 9 above can manage without problem. You can take a tuc tuc back. Be prepared to negotiate the price though. Recommend to visit in the morning or evening. The people who visit this amazing place, never forget to capture a perfect photo when the train goes on the bridge. Recommend to visit this lovely place in Sri Lanka. The Railway times are for Badulla bound ones; 5.35 am, 12.50 pm, 2.45 pm, 5.00 pm and 5.55 pm.  Colombo Bound Trains are :  06. 30 am, 09.15 am, ,10.50 am, 12.00pm and 07.00 pm.

That’s one of the most beautiful views of railway in Sri Lanka. It’s also considered one of the most beautiful train rides in the world. This bridge was built in 1921 in Ceylon, British colonial era of Sri Lanka and it’s made from stone, bricks and cement (with no steel). It’s in Gotuwala, between Demodara and Ella. The bridge is 24m high and 91 m length. To reach there it’s easy walk from Ella railway station (30m), watch out there is a tunnel that you have to consider to check the train schedule to pass this place. Or from little Adam’s peak (1.4km). Check the train timetable to see the train in this bridge. It’s beautiful. You will be able walk along the railroad passing over the bridge. Bellow this bridge a canopy forest and tea plantations plus hills make it a awesome view!

The path is adventurous and easily doable with children and elders.. you can choose to walk along the railway track back to Ella station which is a longer route (30-40mts) but worth it to see the scenery. FYI walking on the track is prohibited by authorities who turn a blind eye to adventures travelers.. fully worth the day trip.

The nine arches bridge at Demodara area is a British engineering marvel of Sri Lankan railway that reminds the famous "harry Potter bridge" or the Glenfinnan viaduct.Now it is one of the most visited places in Sri Lanka. Locals say that it was built by a villager but it is just a folktale & there are enough evidence at Sri Lanka railway department to prove that it was a professional & engineering construction during the British colonisation. It is a wonderful experience to witness the train passing over the bridge and the site is breathtaking as surrounded by the mountains and forests. One can simply walk to the bridge from the Ella railway station (towards Baddulla) and it takes 30-40mins.(Be aware of trains! Do not forget to check train time table) there is a way to the bridge by road and one can take a tuk-tuk too but they may charge like LKR 600-1000 depending on the time. (late evenings or rainy days charges are high) One can catch the sight of early morning trains or day trains or evening trains at the bridge. ( consult the train timetable) Enjoy the place and do not litter!

It is simply incredible to see such a magnificent piece of architecture in the middle of no where, surrounded by jungle. From the main road, you have to walk for quite a long distance to reach there. However, if you don't want to walk, you can reach by car as far as the Hindu shrine (you can also park there and give some offering for the maintenance of the temple). Then hire a tuk-tuk. It will take you there and back for only Rs 500. well worth the money. The ride was in itself an adventure. Never had such a rough ride with a tuk-tuk. Better than any roller-coaster! From the shrine, with the tuk-tuk, it takes about 10 minutes to reach the hill leading down to the bridge. Make sure you reach there at least about 15 minutes before 12 noon. Climb down the hill, following the pathway, until you reach the bridge and wait along with the others. at 12 noon (or was it 12:15... can't remember exactly), the train passes by, preceded by its familiar warning horn. It is an old train model, very charming. Brings you back to the colonial era... It is incredible to be able to get so up close, you can feel the draft as the train passes. Better pictures, however, are taken from a higher perspective, from the hill. After sighting the train, you can go back and have a nice meal at Ella Flower Garden Restaurant, where we also had a wonderful experience. Additional Notes: the train also passes at different times, more or less about every 3 hours. 9, 12, 15, and 18 (but better check the exact time). Be careful when you climb down, a bit slippery, and can be challenging. For children: Children from 9 above can manage without problem. Only need to be with them all the time. We had a young brave boy, age 9, with us. For those who have heart problems: We also have a friend, age 60, who had stents inserted via angioplasty several years ago, and 3 months before he journeyed here from Europe, he had a minor heart problem. Nonetheless, doctors said that he could travel. He came. Did wonderfully well throughout the entire trip (8-days intensive travelling by a rented family car, everyday a different hotel). He too coped without any problem climbing down to the bridge. (He also climbed up to the Rock Temple in Dambulla via the shorter but steeper pathway, without any problem. Later we came back down via the normal and longer way, passing by the huge Golden Buddha).

After the river crossing, take the day path immediately to the left, and NOT the paved road sloping up. 2. Follow the signs to the Nine Arch Lodge. 3. The almost hundred year old bridge is a sight to behold. If you are in Ella, make time to watch trains roll on over this  timeless piece if architecture. It is nestled in the hills of Ella/Demodara amidst private estates and forest. Location: A couple of miles from the main Street of Ella on Passara road, off the main road on an inner narrow road, you will find the view point. There are a couple of routes to get down to the bridge from the view point. If with children, then it is advised you take the longer 30 min route to the bridge than the steeper route which gets you down in 10 min and up in twenty. What to do here: Walk on the bridge, get off the track and take pictures from vantage point, walk along the track a few hundred meters on either side. The main attraction is a timed visit to watch trains pass by. The train leaving Ella will emerge from a tunnel sounding horn and choo-chooing its way into the next turn of the hill. It's fun given the unique location of this bridge. Night skies: If you are here or anywhere in Ella, don't forget to look up.   You will see many times more stars here than in a large city. Close your eyes and listen to the sounds. It's pleasantly different.

The Nine Arch Bridge is an ingenious railway construction built between the railways station Ella and Demodara. It was together with the Demodara Loop the most difficult part of the Main Railway Line Colombo to Badulla and was finished in 1921. It is a copy of the much longer similar Glenfinnan arch bridge in Scotland.  I had chosen to follow the railway track from Ella Station towards Demodara. Boards along the track say that it is not allowed, but it seems that everyone ignores the sign; even policemen don't care. There is another warning sign for robbers, so as I was walking alone I decided to wait for more walkers and walked along with them. It takes about 40 minutes and is a lovely quit walk. Before you leave, check the train times at the ticket counter. Just before the bridge you pass a tunnel. Some people seems to find it an exciting experience to scream inside the tunnel.At the other end you can see the bridge. Cross the bridge, because from the other side you can make nice pictures of the arches. If you want to take nice pictures of the train coming outside or going inside the tunnel, climb up a washed out steep track to a house on the top, called Asanka Cafe. It is a great viewpoint and shouldn't be missed. The Asanka family is a father with four young adult sons. A lovely family.. They make a living of serving teas, coffee, cool drinks and juices. Soon, father will open an open air kitchen and prepare snacks from the terrace. The two eldest sons are local tour guides and very experienced. I hired one for their services. Very nice boys and very reliable. They charge Rupees 2000 to guide you on to Ella Rock, but also any other place in the area. From the terrace in front of the house you can enjoy the most beautiful view on the Nine Arch Bridge, waiting for the train while enjoying your drinks and snacks. A little bit further up behind the house there is a small road leading to the main Pasara Road, from where you can either to a tuktuk to Ella or walk down if you still have the energy. You can also very well extend your visit to Little Adam's Peak with a visit to the Nine Arch Bridge. (see my comment about Nine Arch Bridge). If you want a tuktuk immediately from the viewpoint, you can ask the family to call for a tuktuk. (Rps. 500 to Ella). Tuktuks from the Tunnel entrance charge very high rates (Rps. 2500)

After a nice stroll in the forest downhill from where the Little Adam's peak trail starts, you'll reach the 9-arch bridge. Best view is from the hill above, but the access is very steep and slippery. First of all, a simple search on Google Maps will show this attraction (bridge) as lying between Ella and Demodara railway stations, and closer to Ella. Also less known is that if you walk along the railway line towards Demodara from Ella railway station, you will first encounter the 3-arch bridge, then the 9-Arch bridge, and soon afterwards, the 4-Arch bridge. All these bridges have the same identical architecture, except that it is only the 9-Arch bridge that supports a curve in the railway track. The presence of the other two bridges having the same architecture also helps disprove some of the lore that surrounds the history behind the choice of architecture. At the time of my visit, the cafe situated next to the 9-arch bridge offered the most reasonable rates re. fruit juice and other food. Be careful of the ad hoc cafes on the road that leads upwards toward the Passara and Namunukula roads.They tend to exploit visitors with pricing that can exceed 10 times what other locations offer. Before you go, download the app from the Sri Lanka railways and verify the times at which trains are due at both Ella and Demodara stations. This location is ideal for anyone who likes train-spotting. There is a shortcut to Ella through a pine forest, but people are cautioned to look out for falling pine trees. Photographers also please note that sunset is on the tunnel side - i.e.: towards the Ella side of the railway. Many trains leave Badulla for Colombo in the morning, so frontal shots will have a halation on the lens, unless the photographer uses filters, etc.

We went there in vehicles (as opposed to walking from Demodara station) from Demodara after seeing the Demodara loop. Earlier that day, we took the Train from Diyatalawa to Demodara and was riding on this bridge. (see my review of Demodara Loop). If you're coming here on vehicles, there is a car-park few hundred meters before the bridge. Only 4x4 or small (Tuk Tuk) can go past there due to very steep (uphill) road past that car park to the bridge. But you can walk (uphill) this section although I have to stress that it's steep on good road (most people will be able to do this without a problem). Near the car park, there are few shops, and near the bridge, there is a small restaurant/shop as well. We had some very nice tea from that restaurant. We arrived here at about 5pm to see the Badulla bound "Udarata Menike" training passing the bridge (ETA approx 5:30pm). The train came at about 5:45pm. Badulla bound train will arrive through the tunnel which is immediately before the bridge. Caution: The train arrive and go past the bridge at considerably high speed (normal speed) and it does not slow down here. As Badulla bound train arrive through the tunnel just before the bridge, please ensure not to be on the tracks at that time. Prior to that time however, it's okay to walk along the bridge and take photos etc. Tip: Combine the Demodara Loop and Nine Arches Bridge into a single excursion. See Badulla bound "Podi Menike" train taking the Demodara loop at about 4pm, and then see next Badulla bound train "Udarata Menike" at Nine Arches which passes the bridge at about 5:30pm. Tip: From Demodara station to Nine Arches, I recommend some form of road transport such as hiring a Tuk Tuk so you can use the same vehicle to go back to your accomodation or Ella town. While it's possible to walk from Demodara to Nine Archers, I'm not sure whether it's possible or advisable to walk from Nine Archers to Ella or other towns in the evening (specially after seeing the 5:30-5:45pm train going past Nine Arches Bridge).

A car can go close to this place (a car with reasonable ground clearance). But road is not very smooth.

This iconic bridge outside of Ella is also called "The Bridge in the Sky" and was finished in 1921. It has 9 spans, hence its name, and has a total length of 300 feet. The bridge is surrounded by hills of lush green jungle vegetation which offer great spots for photographing the bridge and trains. For railway lovers a must but also for regular tourists it is very well worth to visit.

On the way there we met a supper cool boy that took us to the best spot to see the view - his house! Was amazing, the views are stunning and he was highly organized with the train schedules and super communicative ! We had a really good time, loads of fotos too and no donations were asked =p

After you visit Little Adam's Peak, consider walking back to Ella via this stunning rail bridge. Continue further along Passara road and head towards a split road on the left - the right hand path leads to The Secret Ella (signposted), the left leads you towards a small water store at the end of a road. There's a quaint charm in seeing the old style trains cross this beautiful archway. I spent a good hour in the area - you can actually take a steep path down to the base and look up. Very pretty. Getting back to Ella is as simple as following the train tracks.

Then it's a steep (in places) scramble done the hill which brings you onto the track.  Everyone walks on the bridge and we walked through the tunnel and took a very leisurely stroll as it was extremely hot at 1pm back to Ella station.  Saw loads of swallows and butterflies and wonderful views. Suggest you wear good shoes/ walking boots too.  Fabulous day, no guides needed cost nothing!

We walked to the bridge from Ella Flower Resort, walking along the main road, about 100 metres after passing the tea factory take the turning to the right and the lower path. This winds down and eventually reaches the railway. There is a good viewpoint part way along this road. When you reach the railway you have to walk a short distance along the track going left and you reach the viaduct. This is impressive and if you time it right even more so with a train going over. There is a train about midday. You can then walk across the viaduct and if you carry on will reach Ella Station in about 45 minutes. The next train isn't until about 1.20pm. There is a reasonable path along the side or you can walk on the track.

This may not be the Great Wall of China or the Pyramides of Egypt, but I still think the bridge was well worth the walk from our guesthouse in Ella. We went to the bridge after hiking up Little Adam's Peak, since it was in the same direction. It was only about 15-20min to walk to the bridge from the main road where you have to enter /exit for the Peak. The bridge is ok signposted, so not to difficult to find. You have to walk very close to some local houses in the hill over the bridge. When you get to the view over the bridge, I found it better to walk to the left out of the path and into the high grass to get an even better angle. We were lucky and got a train passing over the bridge when we arrived there at noon. Some say there is a train passing at 9.30am also. Check the times at the station if you want a picture with a train on the bridge. It's pretty cool both by itself and with a train on it in my opinion. To get back to Ella, we walked on the traintracks through the tunnel. There is a sign there saying it's not allowed, but no one cares... We were not alone on the tracks back to Ella station. Took us about 30min or so. You get some great views from the tracks, and you get away from all the noice and traffic on the main road. If you're only going for the bridge and not the Peak first, I would take the tracks both ways. You hear the slow trains coming long before you see them, so no worties :)

Did the slightly unusual root of going from Ella train station along the tracks to the bridge. It's really safe with plenty of space if a train (as in our case) passes. It's a beautiful walk and definitely worth walking. The bridge is lovely and we hiked up to Akana cafe overlooking the bridge. A lovely viewpoint to stop and have a rest with some tea whilst waiting for the next train to pass. The owners are lovely and friendly. There's also a list of train times underneath the hut (see pic). We then left the cafe to the left and climbed back up to the main road (sharp right). If walking from town (the other way) the sign for the arch bridge is very small so keep your eyes out.

One of the very old bridge in Sri Lanka, mainly popular for the rock design.  It is located  between Ella and Demodara stations. Before you visit, check the train times, you can get some good snaps/videos of train passing the bridge. There is a popular story to say that when construction work was commenced on the bridge. It says that the bridge was built using solid stone bricks and cement without steel by a local called Appuhami. Best way to get there is to start your journey from Ella Railway station and walk towards Demodara - you will enjoy the rail walk for sure. There is an entrance near 98 Acres too. If you visiting the bridge after Mini Adams Peak, then take that entrance. If you are using a Vehicle, turn into Gotuwala Rd from Halpe on Badulla-Bandarawela mian road. Ask from any local guy - they would guide you - road is not the best for a vehicle, but still manageable.

Totally loved this hike - really underrated. Take the Passara Road out of Ella past the flower garden resort. Walk around 25 minutes until you reach the Newburgh Green Tea factory. Bear left off the road and down the track and keep going left for around 5 minutes until you reach the viewpoint. Take some photos before cutting down the path that takes you under the viewpoint through the tea plantations. The path can be steep in places so be careful. You'll shortly hit the railway track. Walk to the left until you hit the bridge just around the corner. Don't worry about trains as they're noisy and slow! The bridge gives amazing views over the canyon below, and there should be plenty of people around to help you with photos and share the excitement of a passing train. If you leave Ella around 8:15 you'll easily be at the bridge in time for the 9:30 train passing by. Best route back to Ella is really peaceful and not done by many - go through the tunnel and take a relaxing on track walk into town. Round trip takes a couple of hours and is a brilliant little adventure.

As on our tour we anyway came rather close to this spot we decided to have a stop and walk there down (and up later) to have a view on this impressive bridge - which from above looks almost like a romantic bridge on a model train landscape. A really impressive and beautiful place to visit. (We had not enough time, but there were many train spotters, who wanted to wait another hour until the next train will pass over this curved bridge.)

Well worth it! Nice walk thought the surrounding area that ends in an impressive view of the bridge. For the photographers amongst you check the 'tourist' train time for a cracking photo. Trains go regularly but the tourist train is an impressive blue colour that pops out in the surroundings. DIRECTIONS: From Ella get a tuc tuc (or car) turning left at Ella junction (as if heading to the start of little Adams peak). carry on the main road round towards the 98 acres hotel. You can take the path down to the left either before the hotel  (at the small Hindu temple) or after the hotel (at the bend with shops). The bend after takes you down from a lovely vantage point. There are plenty of people around to ask directions. For the enthusiastic walkers amongst you, you can also get there on your way down Little Adams Peak. Just follow the signs for the 98 acres hotel on your right. You can also walk from Ella station along the train tracks. We were a bit apprehensive about doing this but in retrospect there is plenty of room along the sides of the track and you can hear any train a mile off so wished we had.

The Nine Arch Bridge is located around 3 kilometers from Ella - almost  between the stations of Ella and Demodara. The bridge has been built of  rock and concrete and serves to fill a steep yet narrow valley between two points on the track. It can be accessed by hiking on the track for around 45 minutes from any of the above stations or by  car  on a rough road and then taking a tuk-tuk or simply by hiking. Since there are many accommodations and other attractions near Ella, it is better to hike on the rail track from Ella. Make  sure to check on the train schedule from Ella station as one has to pass a tunnel and it would not be safe to stay within when a train passes unless one take refuge in a purpose built recess. However, being a remote station, there are very  few trains travelling on this track within the day. It is a good idea to  time your visit so that you can capture a memorable photograph of  a train  as it crosses the bridge.

Take Tour to the Nine Arch Bridge - Demodara. This British Engineering Marvel which is close to Bandarwaela. Take the Badulla route from Bandarawela until you pass the Halpe junction. Just a few hundred meters from the Junction there is an information board that will direct you to the site. It is a very steep drive of nearly 40 minutes.Once you reach the parking area take the concrete road uphill.As soon as you finish the concrete road there is a pathway to your right side. This is barely visible. Take toe pathway until you reach the railway tracks. To your left side there is a tunnel. Go through the Tunnel till you reach this magnificent site. There are nine arches built with stone & cement. Except for railway tracks there is hardly any metal  used to construct the site. The story says that the metal allocated for the project had to be reserved for  War related construction during the first World war time. There is no point seeing the bridge without a train on the track.

Continue along the main road, passing the entrance of Little Adams' Peak, until you reach a Hindu temple with a lane on your left. You should also be able to see a sign pointing to Nine Arches Lodge. Going into the lane and walk towards Nine Arches Lodge and go pass it. There is only one road within so you will not get lost. About 2 turns after the Nine Arches Lodge (right and left), you will come to a Y fork, one leading you to a house and other less obvious one, going down a steep dirt path. We did this walk as a continuation from Ella Rock, carrying on along the train tracks coming back past Ella station. There are signs warning people not to trespass on the track, but we happily ignored these, as do most people. It's a kilometre or so to the nine arch bridge. But first you have to go through a short tunnel, full of screeching bats. You don't want to get stuck in the tunnel with a train coming, so it's helpful to know timings, and maybe safest to listen carefully for a train before entering, and not to linger inside too long. (Although you'd probably be OK if a train came and you positioned yourself close to the tunnel wall?) The bridge is wonderful, and there's a great viewpoint from the far side where you can see the curve of the track and arches. It's definitely worth timing your walk to coincide with a train and watch it pass. From here we headed up the hill, stopping for a cup of tea at the viewpoint cafe. The father and two sons here could not have been more friendly and we had a nice chat. One of the sons was in the middle of building a cabana overlooking the bridge. The tea and crackers was a little expensive by Sri Lankan standards (Rs. 450 for two) but we did get a small plate of snacks and hot and cold tea - and it might have been cheaper if we'd asked prices first! The owner pointed us in the right direction for the short walk to the road leading back to town. Having set off at 11am for Ella Rock, we were at Demodara Bridge just in time for the late afternoon train (1745 I think), and back in town after our cup of tea for about 1900.

To be honest, we set off on this trek starting from Passara Rd, Ella, thinking...well, it´s only a railway bridge, might be a fun trek though. The walk up to the start of the trail is easy and very pleasant. We left early, planning to take tea at the beautiful 98 Acres Resort then meet the train on the bridge. The trail from here on down was tricky and full of leeches, plus it was extremely slippery in parts. We found out later that there are three alternative trails, we took the most difficult one! Crossing the bridge to the tunnel side afforded us breathtaking views - the track and the bridge curve around at an attractive angle offering great photographic opportunities. My girlfriend sat happily on the bridge parapet, with a huge drop below her dangling feet, while I watched in horror, my ...ahem, almost in my throat. I still cannot believe the excitement we both experienced as we watched the train arrive from the blind curve, proceed slowly toward us, locals waving lunatically at us from open windows and doors, then disappear into the dark tunnel. It was a thrill, like a scene from ´The Railway Children´! After the train had gone and the small crowd dispersed, we opted for the hike back to Ella via the railway track. This was also very pleasant. We had time, we played like fools on and off the track, we reverted to childhood memories. Recommend it, but take one of the other less-leechy trails, and definitely - take tea at 98 Acres!

This is a wonderful piece of railway architecture and is also called the "Akasa Palama" ("The Bridge in the Sky" in Sinhalese) due to the sheer height. A 10-15minute walk from the '98 Acres Resort' will get you to the bridge. The significance of the bridge is that it is made out of stones and concrete only without using a single piece of steel apart from the rail of course. The bridge was commissioned in 1921 in the British era but the construction has been done by locals and their knowledge. If you are in to photography, this is an ideal place. You can get some good high angle shots from the little shop leading to the bridge as well as from the bridge as well. The shot will never be perfect without a train and here are the train times. 6.40a.m./ 9.25a.m. / 10.56a.m. / 12.05p.m. / 1.25p.m. / 3.25p.m. / 5.30p.m. and 6.20p.m. If the train does not arrive on time, do not blame me but be patient for a while as trains in Sri Lanka usually gets a bit out of the schedule.

This is the most attractive structure in Sri Lanka Railways. It is a viaduct. Due to the lack of Iron during 1st world war, railways had to build bridges using concrete. This arch bridge was a result of that. When you visit here don't forget to check the railway timetable. Because a train on the bridge gives a fascinating picture that you will never forget. If you want to check the up trains, call Ella station. For down trains call Demodara station. There's no permanent road to access. But there are lot of footpaths. shortest path is from the Passara road. It starts near the 98 acres estate. From there you can walk. Don't forget to ask help from the villagers. They are always helpful. Next path is from the Hindu Kovil just before the 98 acres estate. Vehicles can be parked there. Public transport is also available. Get the Namunukula bus from Ella town.

But still worth seen this and taking some photographs while train crosses the Bridge.

Demodara Bridge (AKA the Nine Arch Bridge) can be reached by walking along the track from Ella station (in the direction of Badulla) or, as we did, part of a circular walk that also takes in Little Adams Peak and the Newburgh Tea Factory. I'd recommend the latter, it's an all day walk but does take in some wonderful sights and views. Whereas in most countries walking on railway tracks is prohibited, or frowned on, in Sri Lankan routes along rail tracks are often recommended as the quickest way of getting from A to B. When we got to the Nine Arch Bridge, a train was just coming through the tunnel behind it, so we stopped to take some pictures and wave back at everyone who was leaning out of the carriages and waving. Although my daughter wasn't standing particularly close to the tracks, the train driver hooted just as he passed her. She jumped a mile. God I love Sri Lanka.

We wandered up here from Ella and it's a really lovely walk! We possibly went the long way round by heading past the green tea factory as I believe it can be reached via the railway as well, but this was a great choice for us as we went past some amazing tea fields! There's a lovely  little cafe at the top with a view onto the bridge where you can enjoy the view as well as refreshments and snacks. DO CHECK WITH THE TRAIN TICKET OFFICE IF THIS IS THE CASE ON THE DAY YOU GO! There is a grassy path along most of the walk, but you don't want to get in a hairy situation with a surprise train. We got to the nine arch bridge by about 8.50am and the blue train went past at around 9.25. There is a cafe next to the bridge if you want to stop for a drink. After the train we kept walking to Demodara station which took about an hour and got there with ten mins to spare to get the 10.40 train back to Ella. Watch out for the bats in the two tunnels. If you like a good old  train track walk then you must do the walk from Haputale to Idalgashinna. The track isn't as grassy, it takes you right across some beautiful tea plantations and the views were more spectacular. The hour train ride from Ella to Haputale is also beaut.

We walked to the nine arch bridge after hiking little Adams peak. From 98 acres, follow the road downhill past a tea factory and down a steep hill towards some shops. At the shops there is a sharp bend to the left down a dirt track. Follow that and it will continue winding downhill until you can see the bridge in the distance. Using Google maps for directions, I followed up a morning hike to Little Adam's Peak with a welcome cold drink at 98 Acres Resort and Spa. From there I continued down the track onto Passara Road, passing the tea factory on the right. After a sharp bend in the road, I took a turn off to the left (just before the small shop) and followed the path to a point from which the bridge is visible. I was lucky. Asanka, a lovely young man with great initiative, spotted me and guided me to his makeshift cafe with a fantastic view of the bridge. The train from Badulla was due (it appeared at 10:50am) and whilst we waited, he and his father supplied me with delicious ginger tea and snacks. I managed to get some great shots of the train as it passed over the bridge and thoroughly enjoyed the company of Asanka and his father who only asked for a 'donation' in return for the tea and snacks. Asanka's cafe is shown on google maps. Do stop by if you make the trip to view the bridge. You won't be disappointed. After leaving the cafe, I walked along the railway tracks to Ella train station. This took about 30 minutes. Altogether (including rest breaks), from Ravana Heights Hotel, the whole hike up Little Adam's Peak and on to 9 Arch Bridge, returning via the railway tracks to Ella and then down through the town took about 3 and a half hours.

The bridge is located far away from the main road. It is difficult to get their. I was able to see this while traveling by train. When heading Badulla, 2km after Ella railway station, the train goes through a tunnel. Just after the tunnel you can see the bridge on your left hand side.

You can come after visiting Little Adam's Peak, as it's very near. Do try to find out the train timings, so that you can snap a shot of a train passing the bridge. (You can ask a local for it). I came at around 2:30pm, and waited an hour to watch a train bound for Badulla passing the bridge. While waiting for the train, a local teenager convinced me to wait at his Uncle's cafe, which had a good vantage point to see the train. Ginger tea, biscuits and fruits were served, but I got a shock when the bill came - 950 rupees! I expressed a little displeasure, but I was thankful for the spot, and for the teenager to also help me with taking some shots of the passing train using my other camera. From there, it's a 40 minute walk back to Ella train station on the railway tracks.

Just a few seconds after we exited the tunnel the train came roaring through. It is an experience that none of us will ever forget. We even felt the track trembling as we ran through the tunnel. Plenty of space at the side of the track for you to move out of the way.  Ignore the signs that tell you walking on the track is prohibited - everyone does it, locals, tourists, everyone.  The station guard did not stop us either. It was about a 30-40 minute walk to reach the bridge.  Definitely worth it, especially if you can time it right for a train passing over the bridge (which we did by complete accident) so check the train times at Ella train station before going.

This is a beautiful bridge over which trains run. If you stand there long enough you can watch a train go by. There is a lot of greenery around it and it is walkable distance to Ella train station. The hike to bridge is also fun. There is a walk way which will take you to the bridge but it is a somewhat steep walk. The walk to Ella station is over the train tracks which according to sign boards is prohibited but everyone does it and is not dangerous. You just need to listen for the train and move out of the way. The trains are not fast so you have plenty of time.

This bridge is one of the most famous ones in Sri Lanka. Yes, it is just a bridge, but still, the walk is pretty good and if you are on time to click a train passing through, it might be worth it. So speak with the officers at Ella railway station regarding the train time table and visit this place.

Highly recommended. The walk there was a bit hot and nerve racking along the tracks but the highlight was meeting a Sri Lankan boy at the bridge who invited me up to his house on the top of his hill for amazing view, where I saw the train pass. He also showed me a shortcut back. If you see him, don't turn down the offer to go up the hill. Highlight of the trip to the bridge.

Get your guide to drive you to the nine arch bridge vicinity i nth evening. it is true that the train from Ella-Badulla runs across the nine arch bridge, but a decent shot might not be easy. There are 3-4 split roads before you reach your destination. Before, you would be trekking in a residential area, so just ask for directions, you will need them. We had to climb down a rather eroded path to get to the level terrain before getting to the clearing and the bridge, it is tricky to negotiate the bends in a clearing with 2 dense forest patches by the side. A local family walked with us and it took only 5 minutes. Take the leap of faith and you will be treated with a fantastic view of the nine arch bridge.

Cool little 45-60min walk from Ella main strip to the bridge along the road past some tea plantations and guest houses and through a small village/residentail area. We missed the initial turn off from the main road but basically after some time you will see a large tea processing facility (i think) on your right and in about 200meters you will come across a small shop. Dont go past the shop, the turn off is about 20m before the shop heading down hill. Theres some construction going on in the area so a friendly local should be able to point you in the right place if you get lost.

To get to the Demodara bridge is very simple; Go to the Ella Railway station, get onto the railway track and walk towards the right. Yes, you will see signs prohibiting you to walk on the railway tracks but nobody is going to stop you. If it makes you feel any better, ask the officer at the station and he'll ask you to do the same. I was dumbfounded when I asked the officer "What if a train comes?" and he replied "Stand aside". It's really not as bizarre as it sounds. The walk along the railway tracks is a rare opportunity if you're from a country where walking on railway tracks is not a norm. It'll take about 30 minutes of walking and passing through a rather dark tunnel before you reach the bridge. Most people would hang around the bridge and wait for a train to come. The train is not very fast and you can hear it from afar. When the train does arrive, do as the officer told, just step to the side of the tracks and get your camera out. You may even be able to get a high five from somebody on the train... Some daredevils would even stand at the end of the tunnel and run off as the train is approaching. I climbed down to the underside of the bridge and there's a small stream there. All in good fun. Tip: Leave about an hour before the next train is expected to pass through so that you'll get to see the train coming.

Completed in the early last century, this landmark piece of engineering leaves many recent marvels in the shade. I enjoyed every minute of the walk along the rail track from Ella Station to this point and found it more than worthy of my exercise.

We were staying at Serene Pavillions and from there its not too far..Going to the bridge is a breeze as its all downhill but coming back up the mountain was not so fun :( All in all, it was a great walk and the bridge was a sight to see.. I have been wanting to see this for a long time and did not disappoint! A must see place if your in Ella. Fantastic place ,Had a great walk along the track ,love this place even the climate,this is a nice old bridge . we waited for 20 minutes for the train to watch that. it has covered with a amazing view. The walk from Ella city to this nine arch bridge was only about 30 minutes.

To reach the bridge we abandoned the minibus at top of the hill as there was no turning place near the railway.  We walked down and down past  small village homes until we reach the track.  Then we walked  along the single rail track stepping with with care on each sleeper whilst listening out for the trains. One did come past but very slowly so there was ample time to climb to safety.  The bridge was not that amazing , a simple viaduct leading towards a tunnel ( which we dared not enter though obviously used as a short cut by locals ). It was the walk, the local surroundings, the laughing children and the total lack of tourists that made it a special place to visit.

Great walk along the tracks to see the bridge and chat with locals during the hike. The walk from Ella to the bridge was only about 35 minutes even with a few short stops for photos along the way. The bridge itself was really neat to see and we timed it well to see a train crossing. Do check the schedules as if you continue on toward Demodara you need to hustle to make the next train back to Ella. We walked fast with very little stopping time and it took every bit of 45 minutes which meant the train was just crossing under the station at Demodara when we arrived. It was close, but we made it. If you miss the train you could always flag down a tuk-tuk or wait for the next train if there is one. The 3rd class ride back to Ella cost 30 cents (USD) and was a real treat. I even managed to pick up a leech during the hike though I had long pants and high socks on (attached to my sock!). No harm though, still alive & well :)

One of the best photos! There are signs that walking on trails is prohibited, but we met many locals along the way, so I guess it is not a problem.

The Nine Arch Bridge is one amongst the must watch places if you in Ella. It can be covered along with Little Adams peak.
